title: Adaptive complete quantum search with unknown number of solutions
authors: Raj Alexandru Guţoiu, Bogdan-Călin Ciobanu, Pantelimon George Popescu
abstract: Unstructured database search is a fundamental problem that requires finding one or more elements satisfying a specific property within a set of candidates. While Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic speedup for finding a marked element when the number of solutions is known, finding all solutions when their number is unknown presents additional challenges. In this paper, we thoroughly analyze this problem by considering all the different regimes of combinations of classical, Grover and generalized fixed-point quantum search instances. We unify these into an adaptive Bayesian approach that maximizes the expected success probability per unit execution time at each searching instance. For a problem with a known number of solutions, much lower than the database size, we prove that our proposed approach is asymptotically optimal within the considered search model. Furthermore, we prove that for any probability distribution characterizing the likely number of solutions, in regimes where the classical verification time is at most 25% of the quantum amplitude amplification time, hybrid classical and Grover approaches are preferred to generalized fixed-point. Outside of this regime, we derive an upper bound on the maximal improvement achievable by fixed-point search compared to the best Grover-based score. Additionally, we determine the optimal transition point between classical sampling and quantum searching using an integral approximation of the probability distribution of the number of solutions. The analytical results are also supported by numerical simulations of the proposed algorithm and by comparisons between the generalized fixed-point and Grover-based search policies.
summary: This paper develops an adaptive Bayesian framework to solve the difficult problem of finding all solutions in an unstructured database when the number of solutions is unknown. It analyzes the trade-offs between classical sampling, Grover search, and fixed-point quantum search based on a 'verification ratio' $r$. The results establish optimal search strategies and provide theoretical guarantees for the efficiency of these hybrid quantum algorithms.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental challenge of finding all solutions in an unstructured database when the total number of solutions is unknown.
main_result: An adaptive Bayesian approach is proposed that is proven to be asymptotically optimal for known solution numbers and provides clear thresholds for when hybrid classical/Grover approaches outperform fixed-point quantum search.
method: The methodology involves developing an adaptive policy that maximizes the expected success probability per unit execution time by dynamically choosing between classical sampling, Grover search, and generalized fixed-point quantum search.
model_or_system: The problem is modeled as an unstructured database search, utilizing quantum operators (oracle and diffuser) and incorporating Bayesian inference to update the probability distribution over the unknown number of solutions.
key_observables: Expected success probability per unit time, posterior distribution over the number of solutions, and the verification ratio (r).
important_parameters: The verification ratio $r$ (classical time / quantum iteration time), the number of solutions $M$, and the database size $N$.
main_assumptions: The cost model assumes oracle evaluation dominates the quantum iteration time, and the search terminates when the expected number of undiscovered solutions falls below a tolerance $\epsilon$.
figures_summary: Figure 8 compares numerical counts against theoretical expressions for asymptotic results and shows the absolute relative difference decreasing as the testing ratio $r$ decreases.
paper_structure: The paper analyzes the problem by unifying classical, Grover, and fixed-point quantum search instances into an adaptive Bayesian framework. It derives optimality proofs for specific regimes of the verification ratio $r$ and determines optimal transition points between search types.
why_interesting: The work provides rigorous theoretical bounds and optimal strategies for quantum search when the underlying problem structure (number of solutions) is unknown, which is a key area of quantum algorithm design.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Two representations of the adaptive Bayesian complete quantum search: (a) pseudocode and (b) the corresponding flowchart. At every nonterminal state, the algorithm selects the searching instance that maximizes the greedy score, evaluates the measured candidate, and updates the posterior distribution.

Figure 2: Selected widths in the finite N = 16384 and continuum trees through level 20, as a function of r: (a) the maximum selected width at each ratio; (b) the percentage of retained posterior records selecting w > 0. Dashed vertical lines mark r = 1/4.

Figure 3: Residual of the maximum gap between the selected YLC and the optimal Grover score for the same posterior distribution obtained from the N = 16384 tree and the continuum tree through level 20: (a) as a function of the YLC depth m for fixed testing ratio r ∈{0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1}; (b) as a function of the testing ratio r over all selected depths.

Figure 4: Complete-search performance at N = 4096, ε = 0.10: (a)-(d) YLC observed search expen- diture (saturated bars) and expenditure after full recovery (pale bars), with Grover search expenditure (solid) and total runtime (dashed); (e)-(f) paired YLC-minus-Grover total-runtime differences over sparse and wide counts. The Bellman curve gives the known-M discovery reference, and annotations give the classical cost rN. All costs use Qq + rQc and all 1024 trials. Shaded bands give pointwise 95% confidence intervals; filled markers in (e)-(f) indicate Holm-resolved differences.

Figure 5: Paired runtime difference ∆T = TYLC −TGrover at N = 4096, r = 1 for ε ∈ {0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 1}: (a) wide solution counts on a logarithmic axis; (b) every M = 1, . . . , 32 on a linear axis. Negative values favor YLC. Shaded bands give pointwise 95% paired confidence intervals, including all 1024 trials.
